about.title: San Rafael Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Marin General and the clinics along San Rafael's medical corridors serve a community of nearly 60,000 residents, and most care here meets the expected standard. But when a diagnosis is missed, a surgical step is skipped, or medication is mismanaged, the harm can be lasting. California treats these cases differently than a typical car crash claim — MICRA sets specific notice periods and requires input from a qualified medical expert before a case can move forward. That's a lot to sort out while you're still recovering. LawProactive doesn't practice law or handle your case directly; we simply listen to what happened and connect you, at no cost, with an independent attorney in our network who focuses on medical malpractice. From there, you can ask questions, understand your options, and decide what, if anything, makes sense to pursue next.

whyChoose.title: What Marin County Residents Should Know Before Waiting

items.title: The Clock Starts Sooner Than You'd Think
items.desc: California generally gives you one year from when you discover the harm, and no more than three years from the injury itself, to bring a claim. Waiting to sort things out can quietly shrink your options.

items.title: A 90-Day Notice Comes First
items.desc: Before a malpractice lawsuit can be filed, California law requires a 90-day notice to the healthcare provider. An attorney familiar with this step can help make sure it's handled correctly and on time.

items.title: Expert Review Is Almost Always Required
items.desc: A bad medical outcome by itself isn't proof of malpractice — California requires a qualified medical expert to weigh in on whether the standard of care was actually breached. An independent attorney can help arrange that kind of review.

items.question: I had a bad outcome from a procedure at a San Rafael clinic — is that automatically malpractice?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law recognizes that medicine carries inherent risk, so a poor result alone doesn't establish malpractice. What matters is whether the care fell below an accepted medical standard, which usually requires review by a qualified expert.

items.question: How long do I have to act on a claim in Marin County?
items.answer: Generally, you have one year from when you discovered the injury, and no more than three years from when it happened, though there are exceptions. Because a 90-day pre-suit notice is also required, it's worth exploring your situation sooner rather than later.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover for pain and suffering?
items.answer: California's MICRA law caps non-economic damages, like pain and suffering, though that cap rises each year under current law. An independent attorney can walk you through how this applies to your specific circumstances.

items.question: Does LawProactive charge anything to connect me with an attorney?
items.answer: No. LawProactive is a free service — we simply connect you with an independent attorney in our network, and any representation would work on a contingency basis, meaning no fee unless there's a recovery.
